evaluation.positioning_hook: A self-doubting teen girl discovers she’s a shapeshifter trapped in a biotech cover-up, then has to outwit the company that made her before it erases who she really is.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean, immediate commercial engine: a teen identity story inside a conspiracy thriller with body-swap spectacle. The audience lane is clear, but the material is more specific than broad four-quadrant fare because it leans hard into weirdness, teen emotion, and mythology.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands immediately in the opening chase and keeps clarifying: a terrified little girl, a shapeshifting body, and a biotech hunt that turns out to be personal. By the time Ava is told she’s been living the wrong life, the premise is fully legible and escalating.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Ava/Madison is a strong lead because the script gives her insecurity, moral force, and a literal identity crisis that keeps changing shape. June, Shannon, Priscilla, and David all have distinct energy, with June especially adding a sharp, blue-collar maternal counterweight.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits to a very specific sci-fi conceit: touch-based copying, memory contamination, and identity as a physical battleground. The Ava-is-Madison reversal and the repeated body changes give it a bold, memorable angle rather than a generic escape thriller.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script is built like a chase movie that keeps reloading its stakes: roadside discovery, school infiltration, mall pursuit, lab reveal, and final collapse into fire. Each act turn introduces a new layer of danger or identity loss, so the momentum stays active.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea feels fresh because the emotional core is not just 'who are they?' but 'what happens when the wrong life becomes the only life you remember?' That combination of body-horror mechanics and adolescent self-worth gives the concept a sticky, ownable resonance.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The small-town setting, the fake private-security operation, the secret lab, and the social-media disinformation layer all create a usable world with rules and pressure. It’s not sprawling, but it does generate story from the town’s complicity and the company’s control.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unusually specific: teen-movie awkwardness, paranoid sci-fi, and body-transformation panic all play in the same register. The script can pivot from cafeteria embarrassment to existential horror without losing its voice.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Under the thriller mechanics, there’s a strong identity-and-class story about being seen, valued, and used. The Ava/June dynamic and the David/Madison bond suggest more emotional depth than the plot initially advertises.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: This is still a lead-driven feature, but the Ava-June-Shannon triangle, plus the uneasy chemistry with Priscilla, David, and Mills, gives the script recurring relational friction. The best scenes are often powered by who trusts whom, not just by the chase.

lead_characters.name: Ava
lead_characters.demographics: female, 16, high-school age, white-presenting in Ava form; identity is structurally fluid because she is actually Madison
lead_characters.hook: The script’s emotional center is a smart, self-conscious teen who thinks she’s an ordinary girl with ordinary insecurities, only to discover she’s a shapeshifting child survivor living inside the wrong identity. As Ava, she’s funny, defensive, and morally stubborn; as Madison, she becomes a frightened kid with a buried history and a dangerous power she doesn’t fully understand. The role is built on the tension between teenage self-loathing and sudden authority, and the final reveal recontextualizes every choice she made.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Saoirse Ronan in Lady Bird or Jodie Comer in Killing Eve — a role that lets an actor play vulnerability, wit, panic, and moral force in the same breath. It also gives the rare physical-performance hook of playing multiple bodies while keeping one emotional center.

lead_characters.name: June
lead_characters.hook: June reads like a hard-luck, fast-talking single mom who’s been forced to become practical before she’s had the chance to be soft. She’s funny, defensive, and economically cornered, but the script gives her real backbone once the shapeshifter truth lands: she can fight, adapt, and protect her kid without becoming sentimental about it. Her arc is one of the script’s best surprises because she’s not just the mom in the room — she becomes a survival partner.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Patricia Clarkson in Pieces of April or Toni Collette in Hereditary a chance to be both combustible and deeply human. It’s a showcase for an actor who can do sharp comic timing, maternal ferocity, and late-breaking emotional authority.

lead_characters.name: Shannon
lead_characters.demographics: female, 16, high-school age, best friend, full-figured, curly-haired
lead_characters.hook: Shannon is the best-friend role with actual personality: loyal, funny, a little skeptical, and socially grounded enough to keep Ava tethered to ordinary life. She’s the one who can call out Ava’s weirdness without turning into a stock sidekick, and her presence gives the script a real teen-world texture. She’s also the audience’s pressure valve, which makes her useful in both comedy and suspense scenes.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of sharp supporting turn that made Beanie Feldstein in Booksmart or Auli’i Cravalho in The Little Mermaid feel alive on screen — a role with warmth, comic timing, and real friendship chemistry. It gives an actor the chance to be the smartest person in the room without being the lead.

lead_characters.name: Priscilla
lead_characters.hook: Priscilla is the script’s best corporate antagonist: polished, unsentimental, and smart enough to sound reasonable while doing something monstrous. She’s not a cackling villain; she’s a professional who believes she’s managing a crisis, which makes her more dangerous and more playable. The script gives her authority, wit, and a real sense of command in every scene she enters.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Laura Linney in Ozark or Carrie Coon in The Leftovers a chance to weaponize intelligence and restraint. It’s a strong part for an actor who can make control feel like menace.

lead_characters.name: David
lead_characters.demographics: male, 90s in base form; can inhabit adult male and female bodies
lead_characters.hook: David is the tragic counterpoint to Madison: a damaged, elderly shapeshifter whose identity has been fragmented by trauma, memory loss, and dependence. He’s tender one minute and unstable the next, which makes him both moving and dangerous. The script uses him to show how the same power can become either a refuge or a prison depending on who’s holding it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Paul Dano in Swiss Army Man or Ben Whishaw in A Very English Scandal a chance to play fragility with volatility underneath. It’s a performance showcase for an actor willing to disappear into body, voice, and emotional fracture.

lead_characters.name: Wolcott
lead_characters.hook: Wolcott is the coldest kind of monster: a true believer who frames exploitation as innovation. He’s not flashy, but the script gives him enough arrogance, grievance, and intellectual vanity to feel like the real engine of the conspiracy. He’s the kind of villain who thinks history will vindicate him, which makes his scenes land with menace.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the sort of role that gave Michael Emerson in Person of Interest or Bryan Cranston in Your Honor a chance to make intelligence feel predatory. It’s a strong character-actor part with authority and moral rot.

lead_characters.name: Mills
lead_characters.hook: Mills is the most human of the company muscle: competent, guarded, and visibly conflicted once the violence gets real. He starts as a threat, but the script gives him enough conscience and personal pressure to keep him from being disposable. That makes him useful as a pressure-release character and a late-story ally.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Shea Whigham in Boardwalk Empire or Michael Kelly in House of Cards a chance to play bruised authority with a conscience. It’s a grounded, scene-stealing supporting part for a strong character actor.

lead_characters.name: Jamieson
lead_characters.hook: Jamieson is the blunt instrument in the room: intimidating, procedural, and always one step away from violence. He’s less psychologically layered than Priscilla or Wolcott, but he gives the script a reliable physical threat and a face for the company’s coercive power. He’s the kind of antagonist who makes every hallway and parking lot feel unsafe.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of a Michael Shannon or Shea Whigham type role — a hard-edged enforcer part that lets an actor play menace through stillness and sudden force. It’s a clean, memorable supporting villain turn.

lead_characters.name: Christy
lead_characters.hook: Christy starts as the intimidating idealized girl in Ava’s crush orbit, then becomes one of the bodies Ava can inhabit, which gives the role a neat symbolic function. She’s not deeply developed, but she’s important because she externalizes Ava’s envy, aspiration, and social anxiety. The script uses her as both teen fantasy and identity template.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Kathryn Newton in Freaky or Angourie Rice in The Nice Guys a chance to be more than the pretty-girl archetype. It’s a useful supporting part with a body-swap twist and a strong visual imprint.

lead_characters.name: Eric Huntington
lead_characters.hook: Eric functions as the absent center of the conspiracy and the body everyone wants to wear. He’s arrogant, self-regarding, and ideologically hollow, which makes him the perfect vessel for the story’s critique of power and privilege. Even though he’s not on the page for long, he’s structurally important because the entire endgame is about becoming him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor a brief but high-impact chance to embody wealth-as-personality, like a sharper version of the mogul parts in Succession. It’s a prestige-cameo style role with real plot weight.

casting_characteristics: one lead must play multiple bodies and ages through shapeshifting
teen roles require age-appropriate casting and careful intimacy framing
supporting roles skew 30s-60s with several strong character-actor parts

technical.vfx_details: practical and digital body-transformation work, identity swaps, and a few creature-like mutation moments; the effect is character-facing rather than spectacle-heavy
technical.sfx_needs: foam spray effects, burns, electrical zaps, fire, gunfire, body-convulsion makeup, and practical transformation support

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release; best positioned as a streaming-first or specialty theatrical genre title with broad teen-adult crossover appeal.

budget.note: Contemporary setting keeps the footprint controlled, but the script still needs multiple chase locations, a mall sequence, a secret lab build, fire, stunts, and transformation effects. It’s manageable, but not a cheap contained play.

casting.note: The lead has to carry the movie while playing multiple identities, ages, and bodies, including a convincing teen-to-child-to-adult shapeshift arc. That is a narrow, high-skill casting lane and the whole movie rises or falls on it.

development.note: The Ava/Madison reveal is a strong engine, but the script asks the audience to track a lot of identity logic, memory contamination, and body-swapping rules. The concept is clear, yet it depends on disciplined exposition and clean emotional signposting.

comp_set.title: Freaky
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the body-swap identity comedy-horror DNA and the pleasure of watching a lead actor play multiple selves under pressure.

comp_set.title: The Faculty
comp_set.why_it_comps: Small-town teen paranoia, hidden invasion, and a school setting that turns ordinary social space into a conspiracy zone.

comp_set.title: The Vast of Night
comp_set.why_it_comps: Contemporary genre mystery with a specific Americana setting and a slow reveal of something stranger beneath the surface.

comp_set.title: Upgrade
comp_set.why_it_comps: High-concept body control and identity displacement wrapped in a propulsive, efficiently staged genre engine.

audience_target.primary_audience: Teens and adults who like smart, high-concept genre movies with identity twists, conspiracy energy, and a strong female lead.
audience_target.demographics: Skews 16-34 with strong female pull; also plays to genre fans 35+ who respond to elevated sci-fi thrillers and body-swap premises.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary locations, moderate VFX, and a mostly contained small-town footprint keep it in indie feature territory, though the chase and transformation work prevent true micro-budget treatment.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where concept-forward genre meets character emotion. The script has a clean hook, a playable lead role, and enough production control to attract buyers looking for a smart, marketable swing rather than a giant effects play.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. The world is specific, but there is no clear franchise or spinoff vector beyond this story.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The hook is immediate and visual.
strengths.what_it_means: That gives the project a fast buyer-read and a trailer-friendly opening that explains itself in seconds. It is the kind of premise that can get a genre exec to keep reading because the movie starts with motion, not setup.
strengths.evidence: The opening woods chase, the roadside shapeshift, and the first public glimpse of the little girl establish the movie’s engine before the title card has time to cool off.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Ava is a real lead role, not just a plot device.
strengths.what_it_means: The movie has a central performance engine that can attract talent looking for range, humor, fear, and emotional transformation in one package. That matters commercially because the role can be the attachment, not just the script.
strengths.evidence: Ava’s insecurity about her body, her moral outrage at the company, and the final identity reversal all give the character a playable arc.

strengths.what_it_means: The touch-based copying, memory bleed, and form-holding mechanics create a built-in set of escalating complications rather than a one-note gimmick. Buyers like rules that produce scenes, and this script has several.
strengths.evidence: The mall sequence, the school hallway touch tests, and the final Eric/Ava identity handoff all turn the power into active drama.

strengths.dimension_or_area: June gives the movie a second emotional engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The mother-daughter relationship broadens the audience beyond pure genre fans and gives the script a grounded human counterweight. That’s a real packaging advantage because it helps the movie play as both thriller and family drama.
strengths.evidence: June’s reveal as a shapeshifter, her fight scenes, and the final found-family ending all deepen the emotional payoff.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The script has a strong contained-genre footprint.
strengths.what_it_means: It’s ambitious enough to feel eventful but still grounded in contemporary locations and a manageable number of set pieces. That makes it attractive to buyers who want a smart genre swing without tentpole economics.
strengths.evidence: Most of the action lives in the woods, town streets, school, mall, house, and secret lab rather than in large-scale worldbuilding.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, high-concept elevated sci-fi thriller with a real star-making lead role and a production footprint that stays inside indie feature economics. The body-swap mechanics, small-town conspiracy, and mother-daughter emotional spine make it easy to pitch to genre buyers who want something commercial but not generic.

items.area: The lead role is a very narrow casting lift.
items.detail: Ava has to play teen insecurity, child terror, adult-body confidence, and multiple identity states without losing the emotional throughline. That is a real attachment dependency for the buy, because the movie’s appeal is tied to a performer who can sell both the concept and the feeling.

items.area: The identity logic gets dense in the back half.
items.detail: Once Ava is revealed as Madison, the script asks the audience to track Ava-body, Madison-body, Eric-body, David-body, and multiple copied versions in quick succession. That’s manageable for a genre audience, but it is the main development friction because the movie has to stay emotionally legible while the bodies keep changing.

items.area: The mall and lab sequences push the scope up.
items.detail: The mall chase, secret-lab interiors, fire, body-convulsion effects, and multiple stunt beats move this out of true contained-indie territory. It’s still producible, but buyers will clock that the script needs disciplined scope control to stay inside the intended budget band.

items.area: The brand and media references need cleanup.
items.detail: TikTok, CNN, the New York Times, Trader Joe's, and the college names are all present on the page, which means a legal pass will need to sort out what stays as flavor and what gets cleared or replaced. None of it is fatal, but it is real clearance work before greenlight.

issues.headline: The script’s biggest friction is not concept — it’s executional load: a demanding lead performance, a dense identity maze, and a few scope-heavy set pieces that keep the movie from being truly cheap. Add a modest but real clearance pass on the branded references, and this becomes a development-and-packaging conversation rather than an easy instant buy.
